title: WHO WERE THE SONS OF GOD IN GENESIS 6?
paragraphs:
WHO WERE THE SONS OF GOD IN GENESIS 6?
The Ancient Mystery That Still Haunts Humanity—and Why the Answer Reveals the Heart of the Gospel
There are passages in Scripture that comfort us.
There are passages that challenge us.

And then there are passages that stop us in our tracks and leave us staring into a mystery so deep that generations of believers, scholars, pastors, and theologians have wrestled with it for thousands of years.
Genesis 6 is one of those passages.
It appears suddenly, almost without warning, in the opening pages of the Bible.
The world is spiraling toward judgment.
Human wickedness is multiplying.
Violence is filling the earth.
Then, in only a few verses, Moses records words that have ignited debate for centuries:
“When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.”
— Genesis 6:1–2 (ESV)
Who were these mysterious “sons of God”?
Why did their actions matter?
What happened next?
And why does understanding this passage matter for believers today?
The answer is far bigger than most people realize.
Because hidden inside this ancient mystery is a story that ultimately points to humanity's deepest scandal and God's greatest grace.
The story begins with a phrase that Moses wrote in Hebrew:

בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים
(Bene HaElohim)
Literally:
“sons of God.”
Throughout the Old Testament, this phrase appears several times.
In the Book of Job, we read:
“Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD.”
— Job 1:6
The Hebrew phrase is the same:

בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים
(Bene HaElohim)
In Job, these clearly appear to be heavenly beings standing before God.
This is one reason many ancient Jewish interpreters believed Genesis 6 referred to angelic beings who crossed boundaries established by God.
This view became widespread in Second Temple Judaism and appears reflected in ancient writings such as the Book of Enoch.
Some scholars also point to the New Testament.
Peter writes:
— 2 Peter 2:4
Jude similarly speaks of angels:
“Who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling.”
— Jude 6
Both passages immediately connect discussions of divine judgment with Noah's generation.
Because of this connection, many conclude that Genesis 6 describes fallen angels engaging in a rebellion against God's created order.
However, there is another historically respected interpretation.
Many Christian scholars throughout church history have understood the “sons of God” as the godly descendants of Seth.
Genesis 4 traces the line of Cain, marked by rebellion and violence.
Genesis 5 traces the line of Seth, through whom faithful worship continued.
According to this view, the “sons of God” were covenant believers who abandoned spiritual faithfulness and intermarried with unbelieving women from Cain's lineage.
The issue was not angelic rebellion but spiritual compromise.
This interpretation emphasizes a recurring biblical theme:
God's people becoming entangled with a world that rejects Him.
A third interpretation sees the “sons of God” as powerful kings, rulers, or tyrants.
In the ancient Near East, kings often claimed divine status and authority.
Under this view, Genesis describes powerful men abusing power, taking women for themselves, and establishing systems of oppression that accelerated human corruption.
Each interpretation has strengths.
Each faces challenges.
Faithful believers have reached different conclusions while affirming the authority of Scripture.
And that is important to remember.
The central message of Genesis 6 does not depend entirely on identifying the sons of God with absolute certainty.
The heart of the passage is unmistakably clear.
Humanity was becoming profoundly corrupted.
The text says:
“The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth.”
— Genesis 6:5
The Hebrew word for wickedness is:

רָעָה
(Ra'ah)
Meaning evil, corruption, moral ruin.
The condition of humanity had reached such depths that Scripture records:
“Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
Imagine that.
Every thought.
Every intention.
Every desire.
Continually.
The problem was not merely behavior.
The problem was the human heart.
And if we're honest, that's where this ancient story suddenly becomes very personal.
Because Genesis 6 is not merely about mysterious beings.
It is about us.
We know what it is like to hide things.
We know what it is like to carry secret sins.
We know what it is like to smile publicly while struggling privately.
We know what it is like to promise God we will change, only to stumble again.
The scandal of Genesis 6 is not simply that humanity became corrupt.
The scandal is that we still are.
Left to ourselves, every generation repeats the same story.
Different technology.
Different culture.
Different century.
The same broken heart.
And yet this is where the Gospel enters.
Because while humanity was writing a story of rebellion, God was already writing a story of redemption.
In the midst of a corrupted world, Genesis says:
“But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.”
— Genesis 6:8
The Hebrew word translated “favor” is:

חֵן
(Chen)
Grace.
Unmerited favor.
Undeserved kindness.
Noah was not saved because he was perfect.
He was saved because God showed grace.
The entire Bible echoes this truth.
Abraham.
Moses.
David.
Peter.
Paul.
Mary Magdalene.
Every redeemed sinner stands on the same foundation.
Grace.
And ultimately that grace finds its fullest expression in Jesus Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:

χάρις
(Charis)
Grace.
God's undeserved favor toward sinners.
At the cross, Jesus took upon Himself the judgment that our rebellion deserved.
The flood points forward to a greater rescue.
The ark points forward to a greater refuge.
Noah points forward to a greater Savior.
His name is Jesus.
The Son of God who never sinned.
The Son of God who never compromised.
The Son of God who never rebelled.
The Son of God who willingly entered our scandal so He could give us His grace.
That is why the deepest question in Genesis 6 is not ultimately:
“Who were the sons of God?”
The deepest question is:
“What will you do with the Son of God?”
Because one day every mystery will be explained.
Every debate will be settled.
Every theological question will find its answer.
But the decision about Jesus cannot be postponed forever.
Maybe you have spent years running from God.
Maybe you carry regrets nobody knows about.
Maybe there are chapters in your life you wish could be erased.
The Gospel declares that Jesus specializes in rewriting stories people think are beyond repair.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted believers.
The woman at the well carried shame.
The thief on the cross had wasted his life.
Yet Jesus transformed every one of their stories.
That is what He does.
That is who He is.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the very thing God uses to encourage someone else.
And don't forget to follow for daily biblical encouragement, discipleship, conviction, healing, Scripture insights, and Gospel-centered content.
One day every mystery in Scripture will be fully understood, but the greatest mystery has already been revealed: that a holy God would love sinners enough to send His Son to save them.
And perhaps that mystery is far more beautiful than the one found in Genesis 6.
The question is not whether God can rewrite a broken story.
The question is whether you will let Him rewrite yours.
The flood ended.
The ark rested.
The waters receded.
But grace kept flowing.
And it still is.
